paragraphs.title: The Pride and Punishment of the King of Tyre

answers: I am a servant of Israel
easy.explanation: He said, “I am a God, I sit in the seat of God.”
easy.q: What did the prince of Tyrus say about himself?

easy.explanation: The passage describes his wisdom, understanding, gold, silver, and riches.
easy.q: What did the prince of Tyrus claim to possess?

answers: Strangers, the terrible of the nations
easy.explanation: The Lord said He would bring strangers, the terrible of the nations, against him.
easy.q: Whom would the Lord bring against the prince of Tyrus?

answers: Because he set his heart as the heart of God
medium.explanation: His judgment came because of his pride and claim to divine status.
medium.q: Why was judgment pronounced against the prince of Tyrus?

answers: They would destroy only the sea
They would draw swords against him and defile his brightness
medium.explanation: The strangers would draw their swords against his wisdom’s beauty and defile his brightness.
medium.q: What would the strangers do to the prince of Tyrus?

answers: A place surrounded by or among the seas
medium.explanation: The phrase describes the place where the prince claimed to sit in divine security.
medium.q: What does “in the midst of the seas” describe in this passage?

answers: The prince claims to be a God, but the Lord says he is a man
The prince is poor, but the Lord says he is rich
The prince is silent, but the Lord says he is speaking
challenge.explanation: The Lord declares, “Thou art a man, and not God.”
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in the prophecy?

answers: They caused him to leave Tyre
They caused him to believe he had divine status
They saved him from the strangers
challenge.explanation: His wisdom, trade, and riches lifted up his heart and encouraged his pride.

answers: Pride, attack by strangers, and death
challenge.explanation: The prince boasts, foreign attackers come against him, and he dies.

paragraphs.title: Lament over the King of Tyre and His Greatness

easy.explanation: Ezekiel was commanded to take up a lamentation upon the king of Tyrus.
easy.q: For whom was Ezekiel commanded to take up a lamentation?

answers: Full of wisdom and perfect in beauty
easy.explanation: He is described as full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.
easy.q: How is the king of Tyrus described at the beginning of the lamentation?

answers: In Eden, the garden of God
easy.explanation: The passage says, “Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God.”
easy.q: Where is the king of Tyrus said to have been?

answers: Precious stones, gold, and musical instruments
medium.explanation: The passage lists precious stones, gold, tabrets, and pipes.
medium.q: Which things emphasize the king’s wealth?

medium.explanation: A lamentation is an expression of mourning or sorrow.
medium.q: What does the word “lamentation” mean in this context?

answers: He was perfect in his ways
medium.explanation: The passage says, “Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created.”
medium.q: What was the king’s condition from the day he was created until iniquity was found in him?

answers: He is described as magnificent and perfect, yet iniquity is found in him
He is described as poor, yet he has treasures
He is described as weak, yet he conquers
challenge.explanation: The lamentation presents his greatness before revealing that iniquity was found in him.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in the description of the king of Tyrus?

answers: They emphasize the splendor and uniqueness attributed to him
They prove that he was a prophet
challenge.explanation: These images strengthen the description of his beauty, wealth, and exalted position.
challenge.q: Why are Eden and precious stones important images in this description?

answers: He was in the garden of God
challenge.explanation: The statement that iniquity was found in him places a limit on the earlier description of perfection.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the perfection described did not continue?

easy.explanation: The passage says that violence filled the midst of him.
easy.q: What filled the midst of the king of Tyrus?

easy.explanation: His heart was lifted up because of his beauty, and his wisdom was corrupted.
The Lord said, “I will cast thee to the ground.”
easy.q: Where would the king of Tyrus be cast?

answers: His merchandise was filled with violence, and he sinned
His merchandise saved him from sin
His merchandise caused him to build houses
medium.explanation: The multitude of his merchandise filled him with violence, and he sinned.
medium.q: What was the connection between merchandise and sin?

medium.explanation: Merchandise refers to goods, trade, or commercial activity.
medium.q: What does “merchandise” mean in this passage?

answers: He was made a greater king
He was brought low and exposed
medium.explanation: He was cast to the ground and laid before kings so they could behold him.
medium.q: What happened to the king before the kings and nations?

answers: He falls from splendor and wealth to fire and ashes
He rises from poverty to wealth
He moves from war to peace only
challenge.explanation: The once-glorious king is cast down, consumed by fire, and brought to ashes.
challenge.q: How is the downfall described in contrast with the king’s former position?

answers: His beauty and splendor caused his wisdom to be corrupted
challenge.explanation: His beauty and brightness led to pride, which corrupted his wisdom.
challenge.q: What does “thou hast corrupted thy wisdom by reason of thy brightness” mean?

answers: It describes the building of the city
It devours him and turns him into ashes
challenge.explanation: Fire comes from within him, devours him, and brings him to ashes.
challenge.q: What role does the fire play in the description of his punishment?

easy.explanation: Ezekiel was told to set his face against Zidon.
easy.q: Toward whom was Ezekiel commanded to set his face?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions pestilence, blood in the streets, and the sword.
easy.q: What would the Lord send upon Sidon?

answers: The wisdom of the king of Tyre
easy.explanation: The Lord would be glorified and sanctified through the judgment.
easy.q: What would become known through the judgment against Sidon?

answers: So that people would know He is the Lord and that He would be sanctified
medium.explanation: The judgment would reveal the Lord’s identity, glory, and holiness.
medium.q: Why would the Lord bring judgment upon Sidon?

answers: The Lord would be honored and recognized
medium.explanation: To be glorified means to be honored and recognized as glorious.
medium.q: What does “I will be glorified in the midst of thee” mean?

answers: The sword would be upon it on every side
Only the king’s palace would be attacked
The danger would be only outside the city
medium.explanation: The wounded would be judged by the sword upon every side.
medium.q: How is the extent of the danger to Sidon described?

answers: That the people would know that the Lord is the Lord
That the city would increase its trade
That the king of Tyre would regain his throne
challenge.explanation: The passage repeatedly says that they would know that He is the Lord.
challenge.q: What purpose of judgment against Sidon is repeated in the passage?

answers: The judgment reveals and establishes the Lord’s holiness in Sidon
The judgment removes the Lord’s holiness
There is no relationship between them
challenge.explanation: The Lord says that He will be sanctified in Sidon.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between judgment and the Lord’s holiness?

answers: It is portrayed as severe punishment in several forms
challenge.explanation: The passage describes several forms of severe calamity coming upon Sidon.
challenge.q: What does the combination of pestilence, blood, and the sword show about the judgment?

paragraphs.title: The Gathering and Security of Israel

answers: From the people among whom they were scattered
easy.explanation: The Lord would gather Israel from the nations among whom they were scattered.
easy.q: From where would the house of Israel be gathered?

easy.explanation: They would dwell in the land given to the Lord’s servant Jacob.
easy.q: To what land would the house of Israel return?

easy.explanation: The passage says they would build houses and plant vineyards.
easy.q: What would the Israelites do after dwelling safely?

answers: Judgment would be executed upon those who despised them
The people would leave the land
medium.explanation: Their security would come after judgment against their surrounding enemies.
medium.q: What would happen before Israel dwelt safely in the land?

medium.explanation: The image describes something painful and troublesome to Israel.
medium.q: What does “a pricking brier” describe in this context?

answers: To settle them in their land and sanctify the Lord’s name
medium.explanation: The Lord would gather Israel, settle them in their land, and be sanctified among the nations.
medium.q: What is the purpose of gathering Israel from the nations?

answers: From scattering among the nations to security in the land
challenge.explanation: Israel is gathered from the nations and then dwells safely in its land.
challenge.q: What is the main movement described in this passage?

answers: Israel’s security leads them to know the Lord as their God
Security causes Israel to forget the Lord
Security has no connection with knowing the Lord
challenge.explanation: The passage ends by saying, “they shall know that I am the Lord their God.”
challenge.q: How is dwelling safely connected with knowing the Lord?

answers: The sword being on every side of Sidon
challenge.explanation: Houses and vineyards represent settled, lasting, and secure life.
challenge.q: Which detail expresses stability rather than merely returning to the land?
